hero.name: Aarti
hero.who: a marketing executive at a Guwahati tea company who keeps postponing her hardest task

story.b: Aarti's day at the tea company in Guwahati always starts with good intentions. The big task is clear: calling an unhappy distributor in Siliguri about a delayed shipment. Instead, she answers easy emails, redesigns a festive poster, joins a call she did not need to join and sorts her desktop folders. Each time she looks at his number, she finds something else to do. At six, the call is still not made. She goes home and eats momos in front of the TV, but the guilt sits with her all evening. She lies awake rehearsing the conversation. The next morning, the distributor has emailed her boss directly. Aarti realises the avoided task got heavier, not lighter.

ask.q: Aarti keeps postponing the most important, most dreaded task. What should she change first?
o: Do easy tasks first to warm up, then tackle the hard one
Do the hardest important task first thing, before checking messages
Wait until she feels confident and the mood is right
ask.why: Warm-up tasks have a habit of filling the whole day, as her own day showed. Waiting for the right mood means waiting forever. Doing the dreaded task first, before messages, removes the weight early and gives the rest of the day real momentum.

chapters.take: The task you avoid gets heavier the longer you carry it.

story.b: The next morning, Aarti does not open her inbox. She makes a cup of strong Assam tea, writes down three points on a slip of paper and calls the Siliguri distributor at 9.15. He is angry for the first two minutes. Then he softens when she explains the new shipment date and offers a small discount on his next order. The call takes eleven minutes. When she hangs up, her hands are a little shaky, but the office suddenly feels lighter. By lunch she has finished two other tasks she had been dragging for days. That evening, she eats dinner with her sister and actually enjoys it. She decides to try one rule for a month: hardest important task first.

ask.q: Her colleague Pallavi has a tough presentation to prepare but likes to clear small emails first. What should Aarti suggest?
o: Clear all emails first, so her mind is free
Do the presentation only after lunch, when she has more energy
Work on the presentation first thing, before opening email
ask.why: Emails always multiply, so clearing them first often swallows the whole morning. Waiting until after lunch gives the dread more hours to grow. Starting the presentation first thing means the biggest weight is handled while she is fresh, and the rest of the day feels easier.

chapters.take: Do the hardest important task first and the day gets lighter.

story.h: A list on a tasting sheet
story.b: Some mornings, Aarti still wastes the first hour deciding what to do, and the phone quietly takes over. So she starts a new routine. Before leaving the office, she writes tomorrow's list on the back of a used tea tasting sheet. The hardest task goes at the top, circled. Then the smaller ones, in order. She leaves the sheet on her keyboard. The next morning, she walks in, sees the circled task and begins before her mind can argue. Her colleague Bikash, at the next desk, spends his first forty minutes scrolling and asking around about what is due. By then, Aarti is already halfway through drafting the new export price list.

ask.q: Bikash says writing a list the night before is a waste of time. What should Aarti tell him?
o: A list written the night before saves the morning hour lost to deciding
He is right, so plan each task only when he reaches it
A detailed list for the whole month at once works better
ask.why: Deciding each task on the spot invites drifting toward the phone. A month-long list is too far away to guide tomorrow. A short list written the night before means he wakes up knowing exactly where to begin, which protects the most fragile hour of the day.

chapters.take: Write tomorrow's plan tonight and the morning starts itself.

story.b: Two weeks before Bihu, Aarti's list has fourteen tasks and every one feels urgent. She takes a pen and asks one question for each: what happens if this gets done, and what happens if it does not? Export papers for a buyer in Dubai: miss them and the shipment sits at the port. High. The festive gift box design: important, but there is still a week. Medium. Updating the company's social media bio and choosing new office calendars: almost nothing happens if they wait. Low. She hands the sample packing to the intern, who is eager to help. Suddenly fourteen urgent tasks become three that truly matter, and Aarti knows exactly where her energy should go.

ask.q: Aarti's intern has a long list and treats every item as equally urgent. What should Aarti teach her?
o: Do tasks in the order they arrived, to be fair
Start with the quickest tasks so the list shrinks fast
Rank each task by what happens if it is done or skipped
ask.why: Arrival order ignores importance, and quick tasks feel productive while the serious ones wait. Asking what happens if each task is done or skipped shows which ones carry real consequences, so she can do those first and delegate or drop the rest.

chapters.take: Rank tasks by their consequences, not by how urgent they feel.

story.h: The report with no first line
story.b: Aarti's boss asks for a thirty-page report on tea sales in the Gulf, due in three weeks. She opens a blank file, stares at it and closes it. For four days she does everything except the report. On the fifth day she writes a different kind of list. Open the file. Type the section headings. Paste last year's sales table. Write one paragraph on the biggest buyer. Each step takes less than twenty minutes. She does the first two that morning. The next day, the table goes in. Once the headings exist, the report stops feeling like a mountain and starts feeling like a staircase. By the second week, Aarti is writing faster than she ever expected.

ask.q: Aarti's friend has to write a long project report and keeps avoiding it. What should Aarti suggest?
o: Block out one whole weekend and write it all at once
Break it into small steps and finish just the first one today
Wait until closer to the deadline, when pressure will help
ask.why: A whole weekend is easy to keep postponing, and deadline pressure often brings panic and poor work. Small steps make starting easy, and starting is the hardest part. Each finished slice builds momentum, so the big task gets done piece by piece.

chapters.take: Slice a big task small enough that starting feels easy.

story.h: What she chose not to do
story.b: Even with good habits, Aarti cannot do everything. Her inbox fills with forwards about office birthdays, an invite to an optional webinar on social media trends and a request to reorganise the shared drive. Before, she would have tried to do them all, and the Gulf report would have slipped. Now she decides, on purpose, what will wait. The forwards can sit unread. The webinar she skips; she can watch the recording later if needed. The shared drive can be cleaned next month, once the report is done. It feels uncomfortable at first, like breaking a rule. But each small thing she delays gives her another quiet hour for the report and the Bihu shipment.

ask.q: Aarti feels guilty about leaving small tasks undone. What is the healthiest way to see it?
o: Choosing to delay low-value tasks is how she makes room for important ones
She should stay late until every small task is cleared
She should do small tasks first so she feels productive
ask.why: Everyone procrastinates on something, so the real question is what to delay. Staying late to finish everything burns her out, and doing small tasks first lets the big ones slip. Deliberately delaying low-value work protects her time for what actually matters.

chapters.take: Choose wisely what to delay, so the important work gets done.

story.b: Weeks later, the Dubai shipment leaves on time and the Gulf report sits on her boss's desk, finished two days early. He asks Aarti how she managed it during the festival rush. She shows him the tasting sheet on her keyboard, with tomorrow's hardest task already circled. The Siliguri distributor has placed two new orders and now calls her directly, without complaining to anyone. The shared drive is still messy, and the office calendars still have not been chosen. Aarti does not mind. Her evenings feel different now. She eats dinner with her sister without rehearsing tomorrow's dreaded call in her head, because by tomorrow morning it will already be done.

chapters.take: Doing the important thing first quietly changes the whole day.
